topic.angle: A horse that seemed to do arithmetic

card.title: The horse that read the room

panels.text: Clever Hans was a horse that appeared to perform arithmetic and other intellectual tasks during exhibitions in Germany in the early 20th century.
His owner, Wilhelm von Osten, asked the questions. Hans answered by tapping his hoof.
In 1907, psychologist Oskar Pfungst demonstrated that the horse was not actually performing these mental tasks, but was watching the reactions of his trainer.
When Hans could see the questioner, he got 89 percent (50 out of 56) of the answers correct. When he could not, he got six percent (2 out of 35).

probes.question: What was Clever Hans actually responding to?
options: Involuntary cues in his trainer's body language
A bell rung by a hidden helper

probes.question: True or false: when Hans could not see the questioner, he still answered most questions correctly.

claims.claim: Panel 2: his owner was Wilhelm von Osten
claims.quote: Hans was a horse owned by Wilhelm von Osten, who was a gymnasium mathematics teacher

claims.claim: Panel 2: von Osten asked the questions; Hans answered by tapping his hoof
claims.quote: Hans would answer by tapping his hoof eleven times.

claims.claim: Panel 3: in 1907 psychologist Oskar Pfungst demonstrated the horse was not performing the mental tasks but watching the reactions of his trainer
claims.quote: In 1907, psychologist Oskar Pfungst demonstrated that the horse was not actually performing these mental tasks, but was watching the reactions of his trainer.

claims.claim: Panel 4: when Hans could see the questioner he got 89 percent (50 of 56) correct

claims.claim: Panel 4 / probe 2 (false): without seeing the questioner he got six percent (2 of 35), so he did not answer most correctly

claims.claim: Probe 1 correct answer: Hans responded to involuntary cues in the trainer's body language
claims.quote: The horse was responding directly to involuntary cues in the body language of the human trainer

claims.claim: Probe 1 distractors (whispered answers from the crowd, hidden bell, chalked numbers) are false
claims.quote: after refuting his initial suspicion of a fraud involving whispering or the like
